transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-11-12 16:00 PST | Duration: ~52m | Attendees: Sophia Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Aisha Patel (Redwood SA); Mark Ellis (Heron Head of Infra), Rina Kapoor (Heron Security), Tom Nguyen (Heron DevOps)

Summary (auto): deep dive on private vpc / on-prem options, network isolation, ingress/egress controls, KMS integration. Next steps captured at end.

00:00 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Hey everyone thanks for jumping on, appreciate the time. Quick roll call, you're all on video?
00:06 Speaker 2 - Mark: Yep Mark here.
00:08 Speaker 3 - Rina: Rina here.
00:09 Speaker 4 - Tom: Tom on my phone, sorry juggling.
00:12 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Great. Diego and Aisha from our side are on the call, we'll drive technical. This is a deep dive per Rina's ask to understand ingress/egress and private control plane options for your security team.
00:25 Speaker 2 - Diego: Great, I'll share my screen and go through the reference architecture. I have a diagram that shows both our Private VPC option and on-prem package.
00:35 Speaker 2 - Diego: So at a high level, Redwood Private can be deployed two ways: a customer-managed VPC where our control plane is either hosted or customer-run, and an on-prem/air-gapped package for highly regulated workloads. The key security constraints we usually see are network isolation, egress allow-lists, and customer-managed KMS.
00:52 Speaker 3 - Rina: Quick question, when you say control plane hosted what data crosses the plane? We need to know PII or any plaintext customer data leaving our network.
01:02 Speaker 2 - Diego: Good call. For the hosted control plane variant control plane traffic is metadata and orchestration only: i.e., heartbeat, instance health, usage stats. Model payloads and inference data can remain in the private subnets if you select Private Data Mode. We support both ephemeral and persistent KV cache options; persistent caches are encrypted at rest with your KMS.
01:24 Speaker 3 - Rina: So payloads never egress unless we opt in for things like telemetry? Need that explicit.
01:29 Speaker 2 - Diego: Correct, by default inference payloads stay within your VPC and egress only when you configure external connectors. We also provide an option to buffer logs to a customer-managed s3 or on-prem object store instead of sending logs to our hosted analytics.
01:44 Speaker 1 - Sophia: And we can provide a data-flow spreadsheet that shows exactly which endpoints are contacted by the control plane, the ports and protocols.
01:53 Speaker 4 - Tom: That will help. On egress we have strict allowlist rules; we can't have dynamic outbound to arbitrary IPs. How do you handle that?
02:03 Speaker 2 - Diego: We recommend an allowlist model: we provide a small set of static egress IP ranges for the nodes that need outbound. For managed control plane there's also a small set of control-plane endpoints. For private on-prem installs there are zero outbound requirements unless you opt-in for auto-updates or telemetry.
02:21 Speaker 3 - Rina: Static IPs okay, but they need to be documented and stable. Are those published?
02:27 Speaker 2 - Diego: Yes, we'll provide a CIDR list and, for accounts on Dedicated or Private, we'll reserve those for the duration of the contract. IPs are stable per-region; they'll be in the network diagram we share.
02:39 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Also, we can sign an ingress/egress SLA for egress IP stability if needed as part of Dedicated.
02:48 Speaker 3 - Rina: Moving to firewalling — do you recommend NGFW in front of your nodes, or do you expect us to rely on security groups + NACLs?
02:58 Speaker 2 - Diego: We typically recommend a layered approach: security groups for host-level microsegmentation, NACLs for subnet-level stateless filtering, and an NGFW/IDS for deep packet inspection and application rules if the customer requires DPI. For banks like you a firewall in the DMZ with explicit rules plus internal host-based policies is common.
03:17 Speaker 3 - Rina: What's the typical port set? We need to align with our firewall team.
03:22 Speaker 2 - Diego: Primary is TLS over 443 for API endpoints. Internal node communications use gRPC (tcp 443/8443 depending on config) and a small control-plane heartbeat port (tcp 15001). We'll include the full port list in the diagram.
03:36 Speaker 4 - Tom: Are there any ephemeral ports used that we'd need to open for dynamic RPCs?
03:41 Speaker 2 - Diego: No ephemeral ports for control; everything is pinned. For GPU scheduling there can be node-management ports but they're on the pinned ranges—again we'll share the exact values.
03:52 Speaker 3 - Rina: KMS — our policy is we own keys, rotation every 90 days, and we use Thales HSM. Can Redwood integrate with customer KMS/HSM?
04:04 Speaker 2 - Diego: Yes. We support customer-managed KMS via standard interfaces — AWS KMS, GCP Cloud KMS, Azure Key Vault, and external HSMs via KMIP/PKCS#11 for on-prem. Envelope encryption is our default: model artifacts and KV caches encrypted with a data key that is itself encrypted by your KMS. We also support HSM-backed signing for keys.
04:26 Speaker 3 - Rina: How are keys rotated without bringing nodes offline?
04:30 Speaker 2 - Diego: We use key versioning: nodes fetch new encrypted data keys and re-encrypt caches lazily; rolling key rotation is supported. For HSMs we can integrate rotation workflows. We'll share the rotation sequence doc.
04:43 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Note: Rina asked about bringing nodes offline — we support zero-downtime rotation in most cases using dual-key acceptance windows. There are edge cases for persistent caches but we can walk through those in the doc.
04:57 Speaker 3 - Rina: Audit logs — we need detailed audit trails for admin actions, API calls, and model changes. Can logs be shipped to our SIEM?
05:06 Speaker 2 - Diego: Absolutely. We stream audit logs to customer-managed endpoints: secure syslog, Kafka, S3 with SSE-KMS, or direct API to Splunk/Datadog. Logs contain user, action, timestamp, resource IDs and request IDs.
05:20 Speaker 3 - Rina: Retention policy — can we set custom retention and ensure immutability for NIST compliance?
05:27 Speaker 2 - Diego: Yes, retained logs can be written to immutable storage or WORM buckets on your side. For hosted analytics we retain at our default but export to your retention is supported as part of the Private offering.
05:39 Speaker 4 - Tom: RBAC/SSO — we want SAML + SCIM for user provisioning and role sync. Does Redwood support SCIM?
05:46 Speaker 2 - Diego: Yes SCIM v2 for provisioning and SAML for SSO. Roles map to granular admin permissions and you can scope roles to environments (dev/stage/prod). For mid-sized orgs we often push SCIM for automated deprovisioning.
05:58 Speaker 3 - Rina: Can we restrict console access to specific subnets or only allow via bastion?
06:03 Speaker 2 - Diego: You can enforce IP-allowlist and we support federated SSO with conditional access. For extra control we recommend limiting access to a management bastion in your subnet and binding admin roles to the bastion's user.
06:16 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Quick pause — any blockers so far?
06:19 Speaker 3 - Rina: No blockers, just details.
06:22 Speaker 2 - Diego: Moving on to network isolation patterns. (screen) Here are two patterns: 1) Fully isolated private subnets with no NAT; all egress goes through a customer egress proxy; 2) Isolated subnets with a limited NAT gateway and egress allowlist. Pattern 1 is the most restrictive.
06:45 Speaker 3 - Rina: Pattern 1 is what we'd prefer. How does Redwood handle updates/patching if nodes have no outbound?
06:53 Speaker 2 - Diego: For pattern 1 we either do air-gapped updates where you pull images from our signed artifact repo via a signed package, or we run an update relay inside your network that you can schedule. On-prem package supports manual patch bundles delivered over secure channels.
07:09 Speaker 4 - Tom: For telemetry — do you collect performance metrics? We can't have perf telemetry leave the network.
07:15 Speaker 2 - Diego: You can opt out of telemetry. If you need metrics we can stream them to a customer-managed Prometheus/Grafana stack inside the VPC.
07:24 Speaker 3 - Rina: Pen test and compliance evidence — do you publish pen test reports and SOC 2 for the private product?
07:31 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Yes, we can share SOC 2 Type II report and ISO27001 scope; for Private deployments we also provide deployment checklists and can coordinate an on-site pen test if required under an enterprise addendum.
07:44 Speaker 3 - Rina: Do you do annual penetration tests and vulnerability scans?
07:48 Speaker 2 - Diego: Annual penetration tests plus continuous vulnerability scanning for images. We also support SCA for dependencies. For Private/on-prem we help share our image SBOMs.
07:58 Speaker 3 - Rina: How about supply chain controls and SBOM?
08:02 Speaker 2 - Diego: We publish SBOMs for our runtime images and can provide attestations for build provenance. Customers can also require signed images and verify sigs during deployment.
08:12 Speaker 4 - Tom: Network logs — are flow logs captured? We need VPC Flow Logs and process-level logs.
08:19 Speaker 2 - Diego: We emit VPC flow logs, host-level process audit logs, and app-level request logs. All can be routed to your SIEM.
08:27 Speaker 3 - Rina: Can logs be anonymized or redacted before leaving? Sometimes logs contain PII in payload ids we prefer not to send.
08:35 Speaker 2 - Diego: We support configurable log redaction rules and PII scrubbing at the source prior to export. That can be configured per-route.
08:45 Speaker 1 - Sophia: User question — what about data residency? Heron is required to keep data within US-East for certain workloads.
08:53 Speaker 3 - Rina: Yes we need east-only for retail banking data.
08:57 Speaker 2 - Diego: We support region pinning across our regions; for Private you can deploy nodes only in US-East and restrict routing. Everything stays in-region, we'll provide region-specific IPs and control-plane endpoints.
09:10 Speaker 3 - Rina: SLA and incident handling — what's the notify/playbook?
09:15 Speaker 1 - Sophia: For Dedicated/Private customers we provide an SLA and a named escalation path. Incidents are triaged per our runbooks and we share post-mortems and relevant logs. We can support SOC calls during high-severity events.
09:27 Speaker 3 - Rina: Good. Any default encryption in transit and at rest?
09:31 Speaker 2 - Diego: TLS1.2+ for in-transit and AES-256 for at-rest. Data keys are wrapped by your KMS. Control-plane traffic is also mTLS if using a customer-run control plane.
09:43 Speaker 4 - Tom: For the on-prem package, do we get the same console or a limited UI?
09:48 Speaker 2 - Diego: You'll get a private console that can be self-hosted in your management subnet. We also offer a private control plane that connects to your console via a private peering link so UI calls never cross the public internet.
10:02 Speaker 3 - Rina: Does Redwood require any privileged access into our network for install? We avoid vendors having long-lived creds.
10:09 Speaker 2 - Diego: Install usually requires a short-lived bootstrap credential or signed installer and we strongly prefer using your bootstrap runner. We do not require persistent admin credentials; all vendor access is auditable and can be limited to a maintenance window.
10:23 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Ok wrapping into an example flow — customer deploys private nodes in their VPC in isolated subnets, attaches to customer KMS for key wrapping, configures egress allowlist to our static IPs or routes through egress proxy, ships audit logs to their SIEM, and applies SAML + SCIM for RBAC.
10:45 Speaker 3 - Rina: That maps to our checklist. Can you provide the network diagram and the port/IP table?
10:50 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Yes we'll send that. Diego you'll also include the key rotation doc and the audit export options?
10:55 Speaker 2 - Diego: Yep will share both plus a sample CRL and image signing policy.
11:02 Speaker 3 - Rina: For POC sizing — we want 2 GPU nodes, 8 vCPU per node, simulate our peak model size. We also want to run a red-team style pen test during the POC. Is that allowed?
11:15 Speaker 2 - Diego: Allowed, we can coordinate a test window and provide monitored endpoints for the red-team. We'll also provide a POC compliance checklist prior to test.
11:25 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Next steps recap: I'll send SOC/ISO and contract redlines template; Diego will send VPC diagram, port list, KMS rotation doc; Tom will share egress IP ranges; schedule POC start date.
11:40 Speaker 3 - Rina: Sounds good. Any final questions?
11:44 Speaker 4 - Tom: None from me. Thanks.
11:46 Speaker 1 - Sophia: Thanks everyone we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
11:50 Meeting end

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mislabels (Speaker 1..4) and minor auto-transcription errors. References: shared links to SOC2 PDF, Private VPC diagram, KMS rotation doc, POC checklist (links to be emailed).
